title: Chennai's Kolu Displays Go Beyond Tradition, From Ayodhya Temple to a 47.8-Foot Record Bid
excerpt: Navaratri 2026 displays in Chennai range from SPR City's 4,500-doll record attempt to handmade home kolus on Japan, village deities and salvation.
body:
• SPR City in Perambur has built a 47.8-foot kolu with more than 4,500 dolls, attempting to break the 36.4-foot record set in Chennai in 2012.
  • Home displays in Chennai this Navaratri range from a handmade replica of the Ayodhya Ram temple to miniature Japanese food scenes and a showcase of lesser-known Tamil village deities.
  • At the Navaratri Thirukovilur temple in Kolathur, about 4,000 dolls include animated set-ups, and organisers say roughly 5,000 people visit each day of the festival.
  • For families abroad recreating kolu at home, the Chennai displays offer concrete theme ideas — one deity, one temple, or one story — rather than a larger display.

Chennai's Navaratri kolu displays this year reach from a record attempt nearly 48 feet tall to a single room devoted to 200 brass Ganesha figures. According to The Hindu, creators across the city spent months researching and building themed displays that move well beyond dolls arranged on steps, turning the annual tradition into miniature worlds built around temples, mythology and places far from Tamil Nadu.

A Record Attempt in Perambur

The largest display comes from SPR India, a real-estate organisation in Perambur, which is attempting what it describes as the world's tallest kolu: 47.8 feet high, holding more than 4,500 dolls, assembled over three months. The target is a record set in 2012 at 36.4 feet. SPR says the height mirrors its 47-floor residential tower in the city, and its Navaratri Utsavam display runs until October 20 with daily poojas and cultural programmes.

https://x.com/the_hindu/status/2111014647314677809

Scale is also the draw at the Navaratri Thirukovilur in Kolathur, a temple dedicated to the festival, where about 4,000 dolls are on display. Organiser L. Gajendran told The Hindu the temple has three animated set-ups this year, including Lord Murugan touring the world and Ganesha circling his parents, Shiva and Parvathi. Carpenters and mechanics began work at least two months in advance, and about 5,000 people visit the temple every day during Navaratri, he said.

Temples Rebuilt in Cardboard

Some of the most detailed work is in private homes. Usha Mahalingam, a 65-year-old homemaker from Nanganallur, has built miniature temples as the centre of her kolu since 2009, recreating pilgrimage sites including Puri Jagannath, Madurai Meenakshi, Palani and Tirupati, along with their surroundings. This year her display centres on the Ram temple in Ayodhya, built entirely by hand from cardboard. She has not visited the temple; she researched its architecture from videos and worked on recreating the way light falls on the deity's face. Her preparations began in June.

"The work completely done by hand gives me peace."

— Usha Mahalingam, kolu creator, Nanganallur

New Themes, Older Stories

Other creators used the kolu to take visitors somewhere unexpected. Shilpa Mitha, who makes miniature food creations in clay at Sueno Souvenir, built a Japan-themed section with dolls eating ramen and gyoza, making hands and legs for the figurines so they could sit and eat in position. At AVM Studios in Vadapalani, miniature cars and a model of the studio's iconic globe sit alongside the kolu.

Nirmala Ashok of Gopalapuram chose "lesser-known Gods of Tamil Nadu" after last year's display on Naari Shakthi, or women's power. Her research produced figures of Madurai Veeran, Sapthakannikaigal, Ayyanar and Muneeswaran, along with other village deities and kaaval deivangal, the guardian gods of villages. A central theme, she says, gives the display direction and lets visitors learn about deities they may never have encountered.

Rajalakshmi Shankar, a 56-year-old social science teacher from Porur, picked moksham — salvation — placing a handcrafted Shivalingam among saints and celestial beings once cursed into animal and bird forms. She says she spends nearly nine months preparing each theme and has explored about 14 themes over the years. In Kodambakkam, Priya Ravi has pared down a collection built over three decades and put the spotlight on one deity: 200 Ganesha idols, each presented with the mythological story attached to it.

What to Watch

The SPR City record attempt still requires official verification, and the home displays stay up only for the festival's nine days. For the diaspora, the pattern in Chennai this year is a usable one: the displays drawing crowds are not necessarily the biggest, but the ones built around a single researched idea — a temple, a deity, a cuisine, a concept like moksham — prepared months ahead.
